Why Zelda Hero Link Doesn't Talk

"And while in some ways I do feel that it could be good to have a game where he speaks, part of me also feels that that air of proud independence he has because he doesn't speak is a precious part of the individuality of his character."

I like this explanation because it hits the nail on the head. I know it's easier to place yourself in the shoes of a silent protagonist (like Gordon Freeman, Half-Life; or Master Chief, Halo) but embracing silence simply as part of the character's personality is something I hadn't really considered but fits Link so well.

I've never gotten how a silent protagonist is somehow more relatable than someone with an actual personality. And as far as valve games go, they always point it out as a bit of humor which further breaks the immersion.

I wouldn't say "relatable" so much as you fill the empty role in yourself. Master Chief never takes off his helmet and has limited dialog so it's easier to forget he exists and imagine that the character's in the game are addressing you directly instead.

I prefer games where characters don't "speak" per se but instead make noises that suit the current tone of conversation. It lets you hear the character's voice in a way and then fill in the blanks yourself, and makes it just that bit more personal, at least for me. So hearing Link scream and grunt lets me know what his voice sounds like, so I can "hear" him speak in my mind if I ever need to.
That's a good perspective; I agree completely.
I think Other M showed what happens when you try to attach a certain personality to a character who's personality has traditionally been ambiguous.

I took 3 years of typing class on IBM Selectric II typewriters back in the day. My first typing teacher would smack our hands with a ruler if we looked at them. Computers have made me sloppy, but I'm still extremely proficient.

I can't imagine not using the "correct" hand placement, although I've known people who can "hunt and peck" pretty darn fast. I learned before the PC era...back in the late 70s. Although I programmed on an Atari 800, almost nobody had access to computers back then. But I had the foresight that it was a skill that I'd probably need, so I took it the first year it was offered (7th grade). Back then we had to use carbon paper and if you made a mistake, it was a major PITA to pull out the correction tape or white-out. We learned to NOT make mistakes. Computers completely undid that level of discipline.

I'm familiar with Dvorak keyboards, but I've never used one. Back in the early 90s when PCs became more mainstream, there was a movement to make those more common. Obviously it never took off (at least in the USA). I'd like to play with one, but have been to cheap/lazy to pay for one. I was one of those kids who (despite taking lessons) never became proficient on the piano, but I was top in my class for typing. I used to practice for fun all the time, and I still do if I get fidgety.

You can switch at will to dvorak and back purely through system settings if you want to. Then it's a matter of printing out a key sheet or physically moving your key caps around until you can touch type again. That said, my understanding is that the performance gain is not particularly large for people who are already around 100 wpm on a normal keyboard.
